name: Wahlquist's Rotating Perfect Fluid
description: A rigidly rotating body of perfect fluid in closed form, its energy density and pressure tied by $\mu + 3p = \mu_0$, which Hugo Wahlquist found in 1968. The surface of zero pressure closes around the fluid, and no asymptotically flat vacuum can be joined to it.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Spin a ball of water and it bulges at the equator. What does spacetime look like inside a spinning star? Roy Kerr's metric of 1963 describes the empty space around a rotating mass, and it came with no body to fill it [kerr1963]. Five years later Hugo Wahlquist, at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, wrote one down in closed form: a perfect fluid turning rigidly about an axis, every drop of it at rest in one rotating frame [wahlquist1968]. His tool was the dyadic calculus he and Frank Estabrook had built in 1964, which writes a spacetime in the quantities that observers riding with the matter measure [estabrook1964, wahlquist1968].¶The fluid keeps one rule: its energy density $\mu$ and its pressure $p$ satisfy $\mu + 3p = \mu_0$, a constant [wahlquist1968]. That sum is the density of gravitational mass, so the body is a ball whose gravitational mass density is uniform [whittaker1968]. John Whittaker published the same ball at rest in July 1968, a month before Wahlquist's paper appeared, and Wahlquist's solution reduces to it in the limit of no rotation [whittaker1968, bradley2000]. The pressure is highest at the centre and falls to zero on a closed surface, where the fluid can end, while the density is lowest at the centre and grows outward [cuchi2013, bradley2007].¶Wahlquist's general solution holds more than a star: it lays the rotating fluid over a Kerr-NUT metric in the same region of spacetime, as Newtonian gravity adds the field of a point mass to the field of the matter around it [wahlquist1968]. Take the fluid away and the Schwarzschild, NUT, and Kerr exteriors are left [wahlquist1968]. Marc Mars rewrote the family in 2001 so that the vacuum sits at one value of a parameter, and there he found Kerr-de Sitter as well, the case $\mu + p = 0$, in which the fluid acts as a cosmological constant [mars2001]. He went on to add an electric charge, and his Wahlquist-Newman metric contains Kerr-Newman-de Sitter [mars2001].¶Why should this one fluid sit so close to Kerr? The Simon tensor, which vanishes for Kerr and for no other stationary, asymptotically flat vacuum field, vanishes here too, and Dietrich Kramer showed in 1985 that Wahlquist's is the only rigidly rotating perfect fluid for which it does [kramer1985, mars2001]. José Senovilla came at it from the algebra of the curvature two years later: every axially symmetric, rigidly rotating perfect fluid of Petrov type D with $\mu + 3p$ constant is Wahlquist's [senovilla1987]. Part of Kerr's symmetry carries over as well: Kazuki Hinoue, Tsuyoshi Houri, Christina Rugina, and Yukinori Yasui found in 2014 that the metric has a Killing-Yano tensor with torsion, with which the equations of a falling particle and of a scalar wave separate as they do around Kerr, though Dirac's equation does not [hinoue2014].¶Does the star have an outside? A body alone in space needs a vacuum around it that flattens out far away, joined along the surface of zero pressure so that the geometry of that surface and its bending agree from both sides [bradley2000]. At the end of 1999 Michael Bradley, Gyula Fodor, Mattias Marklund, and Zoltán Perjés spun the fluid slowly, kept terms to second order in the rotation as James Hartle's scheme for slowly rotating stars does, and found that the conditions at the surface contradict one another [bradley2000, hartle1967]. For a range of its constants the surface is prolate, stretched along the axis of rotation, which they took as the mark of an outside force [bradley2000]. Bradley, Fodor, and Perjés then built a vacuum that does join on, and it is not flat at infinity [bradley2000b]. P. Sarnobat and Cornelius Hoenselaers worked the exterior out order by order in 2006 and found it asymptotically flat at first order in the rotation and not at second [sarnobat2006].¶Other slowly rotating fluids fare better: Bradley, Daniel Eriksson, Fodor, and István Rácz showed in 2007 that slowly rotating fluid balls of Petrov type D form a family with five constants, and that a part of it with four joins to an asymptotically flat vacuum [bradley2007]. The exact problem stays open, and in 2013 Javier Cuchí, Jesús Martín, Alfred Molina, and Eduardo Ruiz wrote that general relativity still lacks an exact solution for the interior of an isolated rotating star [cuchi2013]. In 2020 Houri, Norihiro Tanahashi, and Yasui showed that Maxwell's equations on Wahlquist's spacetime reduce to three scalar equations, two of which separate [houri2020].

related.text: The fluid taken away. In Mars's chart $\beta = 0$, $\mu_0 = 0$, $a_1 = 0$, and $\nu_0 = 1$ leave Kerr's metric, with $Q_0 = a^2$ and $a_2 = -2GM/c^2$ [mars2001].
The metric Wahlquist laid his fluid over. At $\beta = 0$ and $\mu_0 = 0$ Mars's chart is the Kerr-NUT vacuum, with $a_2$ carrying the mass and $a_1$ the NUT parameter [wahlquist1968, mars2001].

The case in which the fluid is a cosmological constant. At $\beta = 0$ the density and the pressure cancel, $\mu + p = 0$, and Mars's chart with $a_1 = 0$ is Carter's black hole with $\Lambda = -\mu_0$ [mars2001].

The field outside a slowly rotating star. Bradley, Fodor, Marklund, and Perjés expanded Wahlquist's fluid to second order in its rotation, as Hartle does, and no asymptotically flat exterior of Hartle and Thorne's kind joins to its surface [bradley2000].
Schwarzschild's star has uniform energy density. Whittaker's sphere, which is Wahlquist's fluid at rest, has uniform $\mu + 3p$, the density of gravitational mass [whittaker1968].

coordinates.name: Wahlquist's Spheroidal
domains: h_1 - h_2 = \left(\xi^2 + \eta^2\right)/b^2 \;\text{(the surface of zero pressure)}

parameters.description: Wahlquist's $r_0$, a length that sets the scale of the rotation; the fluid is static as $r_0 \to 0$ with $r_0/k$ held fixed
A pure number that sets the constant of the equation of state, $\mu + 3p = \mu_0$ with $8\pi G\mu_0/c^4 = 2k^2/(b^2r_0^2)$, where $\mu$ is the energy density and $p$ the pressure
A pure number, $b^{-2}$ being $-g_{tt}$ on the surface of zero pressure; the pressure is $p = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0\left(1 + b^2g_{tt}\right)$
The positive root of $h_2$, a pure number, which is where the axis of rotation lies

Wahlquist's constant $c$, the pure number that keeps the axis free of a conical singularity with $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$: $2/\gamma = \sqrt{1 + k^2\eta_0^2}\,\left|\partial_\eta h_2\right|$ at $\eta = \eta_0$
Wahlquist's function of $\xi$, which grows from $1$ at $\xi = 0$
Wahlquist's function of $\eta$, which falls from $1$ at $\eta = 0$ to zero on the axis

parameters.symbol: W_1 = \dfrac{\xi\sqrt{1 - k^2\xi^2}\left(2k^2\eta^2\left(\eta^2 - \xi^2\right) + 3\eta^2 - \xi^2\right)\arcsin(k\xi) - \eta\sqrt{1 + k^2\eta^2}\left(2k^2\xi^2\left(\eta^2 - \xi^2\right) + 3\xi^2 - \eta^2\right)\mathrm{arsinh}(k\eta)}{k b^2 r_0^2\left(\xi^2 + \eta^2\right)^3} - \dfrac{k^2\left(\xi^4 - 4\xi^2\eta^2 + \eta^4\right) + 3\eta^2 - 3\xi^2}{3 b^2 r_0^2\left(\xi^2 + \eta^2\right)^2}
parameters.description: The electric part of the Weyl tensor in the frame of the line element, $C_{\hat 0\hat 1\hat 0\hat 1}$ with $\hat 0$ the leg along $dt$ and $\hat 1$ the leg along $d\xi$, a curvature

parameters.symbol: W_2 = \dfrac{\xi\sqrt{1 - k^2\xi^2}\left(2k^2\eta^2\left(\eta^2 - \xi^2\right) + 3\eta^2 - \xi^2\right)\mathrm{arsinh}(k\eta) + \eta\sqrt{1 + k^2\eta^2}\left(2k^2\xi^2\left(\eta^2 - \xi^2\right) + 3\xi^2 - \eta^2\right)\arcsin(k\xi)}{k b^2 r_0^2\left(\xi^2 + \eta^2\right)^3} - \dfrac{2\xi\eta\sqrt{1 - k^2\xi^2}\sqrt{1 + k^2\eta^2}}{b^2 r_0^2\left(\xi^2 + \eta^2\right)^2}
parameters.description: The magnetic part, $C_{\hat 0\hat 1\hat 2\hat 3}$, which vanishes where the fluid does not rotate

coordinates.convention: We use Wahlquist's spheroidal coordinates $(t, \xi, \eta, \phi)$, in which the fluid is at rest, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\xi$ and $\eta$ pure numbers, and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$. We write $\gamma$ for the constant he calls $c$, and $h_1$, $h_2$, $W_1$, and $W_2$ as the parameters define them. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{h_1 - h_2}{\xi^2 + \eta^2}\left(c\,dt - \gamma r_0\left(\dfrac{\xi^2 h_2 + \eta^2 h_1}{h_1 - h_2} - \eta_0^2\right)d\phi\right)^2 + r_0^2\left(\xi^2 + \eta^2\right)\left(\dfrac{d\xi^2}{\left(1 - k^2\xi^2\right)h_1} + \dfrac{d\eta^2}{\left(1 + k^2\eta^2\right)h_2} + \dfrac{\gamma^2 h_1 h_2}{h_1 - h_2}d\phi^2\right)

coordinates.name: Mars's Canonical
domains: V > U \;\text{(the fluid, whose velocity is along } \partial_\tau\text{)}

parameters.description: Mars's constant $Q_0$, an area; Kerr-de Sitter has $Q_0 = a^2$, with $a$ its rotation parameter
Mars's constant $\nu_0$, a pure number; Kerr-de Sitter has $\nu_0 = 1 - \Lambda a^2/3$, with $\Lambda = -\mu_0$ its cosmological constant

Half the constant of the equation of state, written as a curvature where Wahlquist's $\mu_0$ is the whole of it as an energy density: $8\pi G(\rho + 3p)/c^4 = 2\mu_0$, with $\rho$ the energy density and $p$ the pressure, $8\pi Gp/c^4 = \mu_0 + \beta^2g_{\tau\tau}$
The NUT parameter, a length
The mass parameter, a length; Kerr-de Sitter has $a_2 = -2GM/c^2$, with $M$ its mass
An inverse length that measures the fluid, $8\pi G(\rho + p)/c^4 = -2\beta^2g_{\tau\tau}$; at $\beta = 0$ the metric is the Kerr-NUT-de Sitter vacuum
A function of $z$, equal to $z^2$ at $\beta = 0$
A function of $y$, equal to $y^2$ at $\beta = 0$
The NUT function: the NUT parameter and the fluid's part, which grows with $z$
The mass function: the mass parameter and the fluid's part, which grows with $y$
Mars's function of $z$, whose zeros are axes of rotation
Mars's function of $y$, whose zeros are Killing horizons

coordinates.name: Mars's Ingoing

parameters.description: Mars's constant $Q_0$, an area; Kerr-de Sitter has $Q_0 = a^2$, with $a$ its rotation parameter
Mars's constant $\nu_0$, a pure number; Kerr-de Sitter has $\nu_0 = 1 - \Lambda a^2/3$, with $\Lambda = -\mu_0$ its cosmological constant

Half the constant of the equation of state, written as a curvature where Wahlquist's $\mu_0$ is the whole of it as an energy density: $8\pi G(\rho + 3p)/c^4 = 2\mu_0$, with $\rho$ the energy density and $p$ the pressure, $8\pi Gp/c^4 = \mu_0 + \beta^2g_{vv}$
The NUT parameter, a length
The mass parameter, a length; Kerr-de Sitter has $a_2 = -2GM/c^2$, with $M$ its mass
An inverse length that measures the fluid, $8\pi G(\rho + p)/c^4 = -2\beta^2g_{vv}$; at $\beta = 0$ the metric is the Kerr-NUT-de Sitter vacuum
A function of $z$, equal to $z^2$ at $\beta = 0$
A function of $y$, equal to $y^2$ at $\beta = 0$
The NUT function: the NUT parameter and the fluid's part, which grows with $z$
The mass function: the mass parameter and the fluid's part, which grows with $y$
Mars's function of $z$, whose zeros are axes of rotation
Mars's function of $y$, whose zeros are Killing horizons

parameters.symbol: W_1 = -\dfrac{n\sinh(2\beta z)\left(2\beta^2 v_2\left(v_1 - v_2\right) - v_1 + 3 v_2\right) + m\sin(2\beta y)\left(2\beta^2 v_1\left(v_1 - v_2\right) + 3 v_1 - v_2\right)}{2\beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^3} - \dfrac{\mu_0\left(\beta^2\left(v_1^2 - 4 v_1 v_2 + v_2^2\right) + 3 v_1 - 3 v_2\right)}{3\beta^2\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^2}
parameters.description: The electric part of the Weyl tensor in the frame of the line element, $C_{\hat 0\hat 1\hat 0\hat 1}$ with $\hat 0$ the leg along $dv + v_1d\phi - (v_1 + v_2)dy/V$ and $\hat 1$ the leg along $dy$, a curvature

parameters.symbol: W_2 = \dfrac{n\sin(2\beta y)\left(2\beta^2 v_1\left(v_1 - v_2\right) + 3 v_1 - v_2\right) - m\sinh(2\beta z)\left(2\beta^2 v_2\left(v_1 - v_2\right) - v_1 + 3 v_2\right)}{2\beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^3} - \dfrac{\mu_0\sinh(2\beta z)\sin(2\beta y)}{2\beta^4\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^2}
parameters.description: The magnetic part, $C_{\hat 0\hat 1\hat 2\hat 3}$, which vanishes where the fluid does not rotate

coordinates.convention: We use Mars's coordinates $(v, y, z, \phi)$ along the ingoing principal null congruence, with $dv = c\,d\tau + v_2\,dy/V$ a length and $d\phi = -d\sigma + dy/V$ an inverse length, where $\tau$ and $\sigma$ are the time and the angle of his canonical chart. We write $v_1$, $v_2$, $n$, $m$, $U$, $V$, $W_1$, and $W_2$ as the parameters define them, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

\ddot{\phi} + \dfrac{U\sin(2\beta y) - V\sin(2\beta y) + \beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)\partial_y V}{2\beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^3}\dot{v}^2 + \dfrac{U\sinh(2\beta z) - V\sinh(2\beta z) - \beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)\partial_z U}{\beta\,U\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^2}\dot{v}\dot{z} + \dfrac{v_1\left(U\sin(2\beta y) - V\sin(2\beta y) + \beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)\partial_y V\right)}{\beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^3}\dot{v}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{\sinh(2\beta z)}{\beta\,U\left(v_1 + v_2\right)}\dot{y}\dot{z} + \dfrac{\sin(2\beta y)}{\beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)}\dot{y}\dot{\phi} - \dfrac{\sin(2\beta y)}{2\beta\,U\left(v_1 + v_2\right)}\dot{z}^2 + \dfrac{v_1\,U\sinh(2\beta z) - v_1\,V\sinh(2\beta z) + \beta\,v_2\left(v_1 + v_2\right)\partial_z U}{\beta\,U\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^2}\dot{z}\dot{\phi} - \dfrac{v_2\,U\left(2v_1 + v_2\right)\sin(2\beta y) + v_1^2\,V\sin(2\beta y) - \beta\,v_1^2\left(v_1 + v_2\right)\partial_y V}{2\beta\left(v_1 + v_2\right)^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Whittaker's Static Limit
domains: X_s\cot X_s = b^2 \;\text{(the surface of zero pressure } X = X_s\text{)}

parameters.description: The length $r_0/k$ of Wahlquist's solution, held fixed as its $r_0 \to 0$, with $8\pi G\mu_0/c^4 = 2/(b^2R_0^2)$ and $\mu_0 = \mu + 3p$ the constant sum of the energy density $\mu$ and three times the pressure $p$
A pure number below $1$, which sets how far the fluid reaches: the pressure vanishes where $F = b^{-2}$
Minus $g_{tt}$, which grows from $1$ at the centre to $b^{-2}$ at the surface; the pressure is $p = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0\left(1 - b^2F\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, X, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $X$ an angle, the areal radius being $R_0\sin X$ and the surface of zero pressure lying at $X = X_s$, and write $F$ as the parameters define it. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{4\left(3b^4\,F^2\sin^4 X + 3b^4\,F^2 - 6b^4\,F - 2b^2\,F\sin^2 X - 2b^2\,F\sin^4 X + 3b^4 + 2b^2\sin^2 X + \sin^4 X\right)\csc^4 X}{R_0^4\,b^4}
geodesics: \ddot{X} + \dfrac{F\left(\sin^2 X + b^2 - b^2\,F\right)\csc X}{2R_0^2\,b^2\cos X}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{\left(b^2\,F - b^2 - \sin^2 X\right)\csc X}{2b^2\,F\cos X}\dot{X}^2 - F\sin X\cos X\,\dot{\theta}^2 - F\sin X\cos X\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
